Senses.Explanation: What is the phrase that threads through the truth-body — the school's standing demand for the word that goes through rather than points, asked of Yunmen and answered with the Dipper, then ruled, re-answered, versed, and smuggled for five hundred years. The origin, in Yunmen Wenyan's own catechism. Question after question runs the gauntlet — the Yunmen sword: the ancestor; the birthplace of all buddhas: ask me another; the white ox in the open: the confronting cue that changes no road. Then: what is the phrase that threads through the truth-body? The master: hide the body in the Dipper. And next after: what is the original school? Not asking, not answering. Dahui Zonggao raises the exchange in the hall and rules on it: the old man of Yunmen, answering thus, answered only the truth-body phrase — he did not answer the phrase that threads through. If today someone asked Jingshan, what is the phrase that threads through the truth-body — I would tell him: a night-market opened in a midge's eye, a swing swung on a great tiger's tongue. And Miyun Yuanwu, raising both at the Tongxuan temple, turns it a third way: if anyone asks me what the threading-through phrase is — a staff across the spine on the spot; even if he does not understand, I guarantee he will not forget it for a whole eternity. The other line of the family: a monk asks Bajiao Huiqing, what is the phrase that threads through the truth-body? Bajiao: first, you may not ask; second, you may not rest. The monk: I do not understand. Bajiao: come a third time and I will meet you. Touzi Yiqing verses it: ask not of Vimalakirti lying ill within the city; Vulture Peak idly shuts away its light. To cross the flowing sands is without difficulty — only do not hear the oriole crying in that grove. And Daxiu Zhu, raising the same at the Buddha-birthday hall and versing: not asking, not resting — the truth-body is not on the tip of the tongue; but let the third coming bring the meeting, and it will run the Guishan water-buffalo to death. Yuejiang Zhengyin, in his own hall catechism at Dianshan: what is the birthplace of all buddhas? Is the Dianshan lake full yet? What is the blow-hair sword? Dust rising from a well-bottom. What is the white ox in the open? Hewing the forehead, gazing toward Caoxi. And what is the phrase that threads through the truth-body? That smuggler of private salt. Then he turns on the assembly: under white sun and blue sky, dreamers with open eyes are as hemp and millet — bring me the dream-thing to look at. You see me talk thus and say the old man talks in his sleep — but when you are not dreaming, what is the thing before your eyes? And Eryin Mi, picking old cases: the elder Fulang, meeting the questioner's line at Yunmen's gate — the master hid the body in the Dipper; Fulang could not fathom it and pressed further. Yunmen gripped him: Speak, speak! Fulang hesitated; the master pushed him away and gave a verse — the cloud-gate tower sheers off the low white clouds; fish in rushing water dare not rest; entering the gate, your seeing was already known — why trouble to lift the rutting mud again? Fulang woke whole. Gripped and pushed away, rolling whole-bodied through the grass; the verse retold, the tongue dragging on the ground — yet the elder who opened an eye right there, says Eryin, is still only a lacquer bucket.
